3.4.1.1-f120.accuracy_reason: In Pliny, NH 30.4 (modern 30.13), 'eam' does refer to magic, and '&c.' does close Burton's English list.

3.4.1.1-f36.accuracy_reason: The Vulgate of Matthew 11:30 reads 'iugum enim meum suave est et onus meum leve'; it is the burden that is light.

3.4.1.1-f38.accuracy_reason: Horace, Odes 3.3.7–8, reads 'impavidum ferient ruinae'; Burton's 'impavidos' makes it plural.

3.4.1.1-f40.accuracy_reason: The Vulgate of Romans 8:31 reads 'si Deus pro nobis'.

3.4.1.1-f43.accuracy_reason: In scholastic usage, totum compositum means the whole composite of body and soul.

3.4.1.1-f45.accuracy_reason: Pliny says Britain practises magic so devoutly that she might seem to have taught it to the Persians, its supposed inventors.

3.4.1.1-f47.accuracy_reason: The distich 'Nocte pluit tota... divisum imperium cum Iove Caesar habet' is quoted as Virgil's in Donatus's Life of Virgil.

3.4.1.1-f55.accuracy_reason: In Brocard (Burchard of Mount Sion), set against the Greek Church, 'Latini' means the Western Church; Burton's English renders it as 'our Church'.

3.4.1.1-f61.accuracy_reason: Convivium is the standard Latin title of Plato's Symposium, as in Ficino's translation.

3.4.1.1-f73.accuracy_reason: This is the correct description of the lictor's office.

3.4.1.1-f80.accuracy_reason: Terra Australis Incognita was the hypothetical southern continent shown on early modern maps.

3.4.1.1-f83.accuracy_reason: New Spain was indeed the Spanish viceroyalty centred on Mexico, covering North and Central America.

3.4.1.1-f84.accuracy_reason: Castilla del Oro was the Spanish name for the territory on the Isthmus of Panama and the neighbouring coast (now Panama and northern Colombia).

3.4.1.1-f86.accuracy_reason: Tacitus, Histories 5.13, calls the Jews 'gens superstitioni obnoxia, religionibus adversa', and Burton's English renders that phrase.
